Almost every meaning of loft as a noun connects to one central idea: something elevated, raised, or existing at a higher level — whether that's a physical space above you, an angle that sends something upward, or a material quality that "lifts" and puffs up. Once you understand this thread, all the meanings click into place naturally.
Meaning 1: A Space Just Below a Roof

This is the most straightforward meaning. A loft is the upper room or open space inside a building, directly under the roof — what many people call an attic.

  • In a house, it's that dim, often dusty space above the top floor where families store old boxes, suitcases, and forgotten furniture.
  • It can be a raw, unfinished space used purely for storage, or it can be converted into a proper bedroom or living area (people call this a "loft conversion").

"We keep our Christmas decorations up in the loft."
"They converted the loft into a cozy bedroom with a skylight."

Key point: It's above the main living areas. You usually reach it by a hatch in the ceiling or a steep, narrow staircase.
Meaning 2: A Loft Apartment (or Simply "A Loft")

In modern usage — especially in cities — a loft refers to a large, open-plan living space, typically on the upper floor of a converted industrial building like an old warehouse or factory.

These spaces are characterized by:

  • High ceilings (often very tall, since factories need headroom)
  • Exposed structural elements — bare brick walls, visible pipes, wooden beams
  • Wide, open floor plans with few or no interior walls
  • Large windows

They became fashionable in cities like New York, London, and Chicago, where artists first moved into abandoned industrial buildings because the rents were cheap and the spaces were huge. Today, "loft-style" is considered a trendy, desirable aesthetic.

"She lives in a loft downtown — you walk in and it's just one enormous open space with these massive windows."
"The loft had exposed brick on every wall and ceilings so high you'd need a ladder to change a bulb."

In farming contexts, a loft (or hayloft) is the upper level of a barn, used to store hay. It sits above the area where the animals are kept on the ground floor. Hay was tossed or pitched down from the loft to the animals below.

"The children climbed up to the hayloft and jumped into the piles of straw."

This is the oldest and most traditional use of the word in rural life.

A pigeon loft is a specially built structure (like a small shed or housing unit) where pigeons are kept, particularly racing pigeons or carrier pigeons. It's their home — where they roost, breed, and return to after being released miles away.

"He's been keeping racing pigeons in his loft for over thirty years."

You'll often just hear pigeon keepers say "the loft" when referring to this structure.
Meaning 5: A Gallery Inside a Church

In architecture, a loft can refer to a raised gallery or platform inside a church or large hall. Two common examples:

  • Organ loft — the elevated platform where the pipe organ and organist are situated, usually high up at the back or side of a church.
  • Choir loft — the raised area where the choir sings.

Think of it as a balcony-like structure built into the upper part of the interior. The elevation serves a purpose: sound travels better from height, and it keeps the musicians/singers visible and separate from the congregation.

"The choir sang from the loft above, and the sound cascaded down beautifully."
Meaning 6: The Angle of a Golf Club's Face (Golf)

In golf, loft refers to the angle of the face of a golf club — that is, how much the face tilts backward from vertical. This angle is what determines how high the ball travels when hit.

  • A club with high loft (like a wedge) sends the ball steeply upward and doesn't cover much horizontal distance.
  • A club with low loft (like a driver) sends the ball on a flatter, lower trajectory and covers much greater distance.

"Use a club with more loft if you need the ball to clear that bunker."
"The 9-iron has significantly more loft than the 3-iron."

This meaning connects perfectly to the core idea — loft is literally what lifts the ball into the air.
Meaning 7: The Fluffiness or Thickness of a Material

This is a slightly technical but very useful meaning. In the context of bedding, sleeping bags, down jackets, and insulation materials, loft refers to the ability of a material to puff up, expand, and trap air — and by extension, how thick and fluffy it is.

  • High loft = the material is thick, airy, and full — it traps a lot of air, and air is an excellent insulator, so high-loft materials keep you very warm.
  • Low loft = the material is flat, compressed, and thin — it traps less air and keeps you less warm.

You'll often see this on product labels:

"This sleeping bag has 800-fill-power down with excellent loft — perfect for winter camping."
"After washing, the duvet lost some of its loft and felt flatter than before."

Think of a freshly fluffed pillow vs. a flat, squashed one. The fluffy one has high loft. The core idea again: loft = lift, height, puffiness.
